title: CVE-2026-108963 - Databasement Argument Injection Remote Code Execution
text:
8.8

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-108963
Databasement Argument Injection Remote Code Execution

databasement before 1.8.2 allows remote code execution because it runs certain commands (e.g., mariadb-dump) with a database name that can be specified by any authenticated user. For example, --result-file=/app/public/index.php can write to index.php. In other words, quoting prevents OS command injection in mariadb-dump, but the argument injection alone is sufficient for code execution indirectly. NOTE: the project's composer.json file does not indicate an independently published databasement Composer package.

Bitdefender finds Midnight Mimosa, preinstalled Android malware on cheap MediaTek phones that fakes ad clicks, drops apps and builds a proxy botnet.

Bitdefender researchers discovered a campaign called Midnight Mimosa involving preinstalled Android malware on low-cost phones from different brands that use MediaTek platforms. The malware is built into the device firmware and may be hidden in different system packages depending on the model. It is already on the phone before the owner turns it on for the first time and cannot be removed.

The malware has system-level privileges, allowing it to install and remove apps, grant permissions and download code from a remote server without the user’s knowledge. This gives its operators control over the infected devices and allows them to use them for different purposes, including building a large botnet. The campaign appears to be mainly financially motivated.

“This scheme is likely designed mainly to generate revenue. The operators carry out ad and click fraud, collect device and installed-app information, and turn infected devices into residential-proxy relay nodes, making them zombies in botnets.” Bitdefender states. “This creates an additional revenue stream, as access to botnets for DDoS attacks is a hot commodity. title: GhostAction Phishing Campaign
text:
Jump to section· ContactTwo days ago, in our last blog post, we warned our readers that the GhostAction threat actor had registered a new domain my-github[.]com and we theorized that they were intending to use it for phishing. Unfortunately, we were right: the GhostAction campaign has moved beyond malicious GitHub Actions workflows and into direct, personalized phishing of open-source developers. OpenSourceMalware obtained a phishing email presented as coming from noreply@my-github[.]com that impersonated a GitHub security alert, addressed the recipient by name, and urged them to secure their account through a unique-looking path on the lookalike domain.Recovered page source shows this was more than a password form. The site acted as a GitHub reverse proxy, collected the victim’s password and authenticator code, and injected JavaScript that silently authorized a GitHub OAuth device flow with repo, workflow, and read:org scopes. The script then sent the resulting access token to my-github[.]com on TCP/8443. Those permissions align directly with GhostAction’s ability to enumerate repositories and inject malicious workflow files.The link is the critical connection. my-github[.]com resolves to 193.32.204[.]199, the same server used by the latest GhostAction workflows to receive stolen CI/CD and repository credentials. The email used https://my-github[.]com/SDRVuhYw, the exact path that appeared in public scanning hours after the domain was registered. Technical Analysis
Vearch is a distributed vector search system that exposes a REST API for document ingestion, querying, and cluster administration. The vulnerable component is the authorization logic inside Role.HasPermissionForResources. According to the NVD description, this function "ignores stored ReadOnly or None privilege levels for resources listed in a role." In other words, when a role grants a user read access (ReadOnly) to a resource, the permission check fails to honor that restriction and instead permits operations that require higher privileges. Likewise, a None privilege — which should deny access entirely — is not enforced.
The root cause maps to CWE-863 (Incorrect Authorization): the authorization decision is made without correctly evaluating the stored privilege metadata attached to a role. This is a server-side access-control defect, not a memory-safety or injection issue. The attack surface is the Vearch HTTP API, which is authenticated — the CVSS vector (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N) confirms the attacker already holds low-privileged credentials but can reach the service over the network with no user interaction.
Because the flaw affects the general permission-checking routine rather than a single endpoint, its consequences propagate across every API operation that relies on HasPermissionForResources. The NVD description explicitly names two abuse paths: (1) upserting and deleting documents with read-only access, and (2) calling PUT /roles to grant the attacker's own role WriteRead privileges. The second path is the more severe because it converts a horizontal privilege problem into a vertical one — role self-modification that trends toward cluster administrator access.
No source code, advisory, or PoC was provided in the intelligence feed, so the exact code branch that mishandles the privilege comparison cannot be quoted. The vulnerability class and its two documented abuse paths are sufficient to define detection and mitigation, but readers should treat any finer-grained implementation claim as unverified. Notably, the version range ends at 3.5.9 with no fix release identified, meaning all versions from 3.5.2 through 3.5.9 are believed affected.

AI-Built Torrent Site Looks Inside Downloads to Catch Fakes and Malware

TorrentClaw is a relatively new torrent search engine that launched in February.
The site is built on links from its own DHT crawler and dozens of external torrent sites and aggregators. In just a few months, the site has grown into an index of more than six million torrents, including the latest Hollywood blockbusters and hit series.
The homepage looks more modern than traditional torrent sites and has some clear AI-design tells. That’s not a secret. On the contrary, AI plays a central role in the site’s development and marketing.
TorrentClaw.com

According to TorrentClaw’s developers, who all use the name Deivid Soto, the platform is largely built and run with the help of AI.
“Basically, the core framework is Claude Code combined with local LLMs for specific execution and ingestion tasks,” Soto tells us.
For example, AI is used to match torrents to film and TV titles, so these can be neatly organized. The AI-driven categorization process takes over tasks that would otherwise be manual work, and AI helped to build novel tools as well.
One of the features built this way is TrueSpec, which checks whether torrents actually contain what their names suggest. That helps to spot fake torrents and malware.
TrueSpec: Download and Verify
On most torrent sites, release names are the main source of information for torrent users. They list the resolution, codec, audio and release group, but there’s no guarantee that any of it is accurate.
Mislabeled torrents are often handled by moderators on well-run torrent sites, but most automated indexes have no active moderation. That’s where TrueSpec comes in.
TrueSpec joins the torrent swarm, reads the file listing, and downloads enough pieces to check the video with the analysis tool ffprobe. According to the site and its developers, that’s between 10 and 20 MB per torrent.
TrueSpec

In addition to verifying the names, TrueSpec also checks suspicious files. It looks up their hashes on VirusTotal and, if the files are small enough, uploads these for a scan. TorrentClaw doesn’t run its own virus scanner, the malware verdicts come from VirusTotal.
When TrueSpec finds malware, the torrent remains listed on the site, but with a “Malware detected” label and the download button disabled. At the time of writing, one fake Jujutsu Kaisen episode with this label still had 34 seeders while it remained available on some external sites.
‘Malware detected’

Not Perfect
The TrueSpec system isn’t perfect. In July, an earlier dataset counted 6,450 malware cases, but many were false positives. These included the harmless RARBG_DO_NOT_MIRROR.exe file, fansub scripts that switch audio languages, and scripts that simply open a website.
The TrueSpec data from late September paints a different picture. TorrentClaw now only counts malware when VirusTotal confirms it, which leaves 34 torrents. We checked some of these against the evidence in the data, which links to a VirusTotal report for every confirmed case.
Detected malware is rare, but the count is likely too low. TrueSpec doesn’t download large executables, it prioritizes well-seeded torrents, and dead swarms can’t be checked at all. TorrentClaw also focuses on films and TV shows, so pirated software and games are largely left out.
Malware is only part of what TrueSpec flags. In total, 1,265 of the 687,057 probed torrents were flagged as deceptive, including programs disguised as videos and fake resolutions. That’s less than 0.2% of all checked torrents.
The most common type of ‘mislabeling’ is actually quite harmless. More than half of all probed torrents, 55%, include subtitle tracks that their release names don’t mention. TorrentClaw flags this as a missing label, but subtitles are typically not added to titles unless they are hardcoded. Scene rules don’t require this either.
VLC Player Malware

text: Subscribe Cyber Cognition BlogAll PostsAre We Actually Getting Better at Cyber Defence?6 April 2026|Cyber Security, Systems ThinkingImage by freepikHere's a question the security industry is surprisingly bad at asking directly: are we actually getting better?Not better at spending, or adopting frameworks, or buying tools. Better at the thing security is supposed to do like preventing harm and containing loss when prevention fails.I've been sitting with data from the Cyentia Institute's IRIS 2025 report which covers 15 years of real incident loss data, sponsored by CISA, covering organisations across size and sector. It's one of the most rigorous attempts to measure security outcomes I've come across. Not vendor surveys. Not self-reported maturity scores. Actual financial losses from actual incidents, tracked across time.The numbers are not flattering.The Measurement TrapBefore we look at what Cyentia found, it's worth understanding why this question is so hard to answer honestly. The security industry is extraordinarily good at measuring inputs. Annual security spend. Number of tools deployed. Frameworks adopted. Staff certified. Vulnerabilities patched within SLA. Phishing click rates after training. We produce dashboards full of this and report it upward with quiet confidence.None of it directly measures whether the system is working.Activity is not the same as outcome. Spend is not the same as effectiveness. A framework adoption rate tells you something about compliance behaviour — it tells you almost nothing about whether harm is being prevented or reduced.We've built an entire reporting culture around the things that are easy to count. Because we count them, we assume they represent progress.That assumption deserves scrutiny. Because we have 15 years of outcome data now. And it suggests the assumption is wrong.What the Data Actually SaysThe Cyentia IRIS 2025 report tracks financial losses from security incidents across 15 years. Here's what it found.Median incident cost has increased roughly 15 times over that period. Adjusted for inflation. So we're not talking about nominal dollar growth — real losses have grown from around $190,000 to approximately $3 million at the median.That's not a marginal trend. That's a structural one.But the median only tells part of the story. Losses relative to annual revenue have grown 8 times over the same period. This matters because it strips out the "organisations are bigger and more valuable now" argument. Even as a proportion of what organisations generate, losses have grown dramatically. Security incidents are costing more relative to what organisations are worth and what they produce.At the extreme end, the 90th percentile of loss events, costs have grown roughly 5 times. The worst events are getting worse too, not just the typical ones.And the small organisation finding is worth dwelling on. Absolute losses are higher at large organisations — that's intuitive, bigger systems, more assets, more complexity. But the relative impact is significantly worse for smaller firms. They're losing more as a proportion of revenue and they have far less capacity to absorb it. For the top 5% of loss events, costs can exceed the annual revenue of the affected organisation. Not a bad quarter. A potentially existential event.Think about what that means for a moment.A System Producing These Outcomes Isn't LuckyThis is where the framing shifts completely if you apply a systems thinking lens.A system that produces 15 years of worsening outcomes isn't having a run of bad luck. It's operating exactly as designed. The outputs are emergent properties of how the system is structured, the incentives, the measurement models, the feedback loops, the relationships between the parts that make it up.We've drawn a very particular boundary around "cybersecurity." # FBI Arrest of Ransomware Negotiator Disrupts ShinyHunters After 20 Incidents This Week

The FBI picked up a ransomware negotiator in Philadelphia this week, but that's not the real story here. It's more of a peek at how shaky the logistics are for people who steal data. Everyone is looking at the handcuffs, but look at the volume instead. ShinyHunters has been all over the news lately with 20 different stories tied to them.

If you've been following them, you'll see they don't play the usual "lock and leak" game. They aren't interested in freezing your servers and waiting for Bitcoin to let you back in. Instead, they go for the massive haul. Think of it as hunting for a gold mine of search histories and personal info. Take the ASOS breach from this week. That's their signature. They find a way into a high-value data store, grab everything, and then threaten to make it public.

We have to be careful with how we name these people, though. On leak sites, "ShinyHunters" is less of a specific gang and more of a brand for high-end theft. When a polished data dump hits a forum, analysts just slap that label on it. Is it likely that 20 different stories point to the same five people in one room? Probably not. It's more like a loose group of access brokers and extortionists sharing the same tools.

How do these dumps actually happen? This is where those claims about "military-grade" encryption usually fall apart. When these groups hit a database, they aren't trying to break AES-256 encryption on the disk. That would be useless. Instead, they steal session tokens or find an API that isn't configured right to get data that's already been decrypted.

For any sysadmins out there, remember that the algorithm isn't your biggest problem. It's how you handle the keys. If you keep your encryption keys in a plaintext config file on the same server as your data, your cipher doesn't matter. Why buy a vault door from a Swiss engineer just to leave the key under the welcome mat?

To actually stop this, we need Key Stretching. When users make passwords, we shouldn't just hash them; we should use Argon2 or PBKDF2. The goal is to make the process slow on purpose. A user won't notice a 100 millisecond delay. But for an attacker with 8.6 million records, like in the Nippon Columbia incident, that tiny delay becomes a wall. It turns a database into a nightmare for any computer trying to crack it. Claude Shannon taught us that information is the resolution of uncertainty. By making the work harder, we make sure that solving the puzzle stays expensive.

We're seeing what happens when these actors target service providers over in Japan. The attack on IDCF Cloud didn't just hit one office; it affected 495 organizations, including JR East. When you hit a cloud provider, you aren't just hitting one victim. You're hitting the whole supply chain. If a major city's transport depends on a compromised cloud instance, is that still just a legal problem? No, it's a logistics crisis.

Some people think the Philadelphia arrest is just symbolic and won't slow anyone down because these groups are decentralized. They've mostly got a point. Taking out one negotiator doesn't kill the whole operation. But it does add friction. Ransomware is a business. When you mess with the payment pipeline or the negotiations, you lower the return on investment for the attacker.

Fixing this doesn't require some fancy AI security suite. It just takes the boring work of rotating secrets and using a proper Key Management Service. Moving keys out of the app environment and into a managed vault or an HSM costs a few thousand dollars in licenses and some time to fix the code.

It is significantly cheaper than the $177 million settlement AT&T just finalized for its own breach.

These flaws gained attention after an autonomous AI agent chained them to breach the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) in September 2026.Vulnerabilities summary:CVE-2026-102489 (CVSS score 9.6) - a session fixation vulnerability allows attackers to hijack active user sessions and run malicious code with the privileges of the Zammad service. The flaw is in the software's session management logic and enables remote code execution without requiring valid credentials. It specifically targets the runtime environment of older versions to gain a foothold on the system.CVE-2026-102490 (CVSS score 9.8) - a local privilege escalation vulnerability allows a low-privileged user to gain root access on the underlying Linux server. The issue stems from improper privilege management in packages built via packager.io where service processes run as root before dropping identities. Attackers who have already gained access to the Zammad service account can use this flaw to take complete control of the host within seconds.The impact of these vulnerabilities is significant because helpdesk systems often store sensitive customer data and internal IT tickets. A successful exploit allows attackers to take complete control of the host and access all stored information.The vulnerabilities affect a range of Zammad installations depending on the specific flaw and package type. CVE-2026-102489 is practically exploitable in versions 6.3.0 through 6.5.4. Although the code is present in versions 7.0.0 to 7.1.3, environment changes make it difficult to exploit in those releases.CVE-2026-102490 affects all Zammad versions distributed as DEB or RPM packages, but source-based and container-based installations remain unaffected.Administrators must update their Zammad installations to version 7.2.0 or later. Organizations should also restrict server access to trusted administrators and place the helpdesk within a secure network segment.If a system shows signs of compromise, administrators should rebuild the host and rotate all credentials, including mailbox passwords and API tokens.

title: The Luna Moth Files Weren’t Hacked. Here’s How They Leaked.
text:
When asked about the “Luna Moth Files” that had mysteriously appeared online, Silent Ransom Group called them “fake” and insisted they hadn’t had any leak or breach. But they had. Here’s what we know.  
When the “Luna Moth Files” appeared on an onion site without anyone claiming responsibility or explaining their origin, DataBreaches asked a spokesperson for Silent Ransom Group (SRG) to comment on the leak. To our surprise, they denied any leak, telling DataBreaches, “… SRG was never leaked. We have never been hacked or had a data breach. We have come across false articles claiming that we were hacked and that our chat logs were published.”
They may never have been hacked, but they definitely had a leak, and this incident belongs in our “No Need to Hack When It’s Leaking” series.
A message from a researcher
In response to our previous report encouraging people with knowledge of the incident to contact us, a researcher we have known for years reached out. They did not claim to have leaked the data. Instead, they said they were NOT the person or people who leaked it, but they knew the data’s source. By agreement, we are not naming them to protect them from possible retaliation.
“Looks like it was not only me who discovered their open server with chats,” they wrote.
They told us that in August, 2026 they discovered a misconfigured MongoDB instance that left the user’s Rocket.Chat records exposed. The exposed data were not secured until after September 28, 2026, which was the last re-check the researcher did and at which time, the data were still exposed.
Screenshots provided by the researcher and redacted by DataBreaches show that on August 24, 2026, and September 28, 2016,  Rocket.Chat data were exposed on an IP address in Lithuania.

Screenshots show that the MongoDB “rocketchat” was open when checked on August 24, 2026, and September 28, 2026—screenshots redacted by DataBreaches.net. 
According to the researcher, the data in the published Luna Moth Files exactly matched what the researcher discovered. Since the last date in the leaked files was September 29, it was probably secured on that date.
What we know and what we still don’t know
To be clear, access to Rocket.Chat was secured with passwords, and we are not aware of any credential leak. But SRG’s MongoDB backup was passwordless, so all the content in the backup, including the Rocket.Chats, was publicly available.
DataBreaches does not know who leaked the files publicly. The first reference we found to the “Luna Moth Files” was an October 3 post on X.com by DonaldHame0q, but we don’t know for sure whether they leaked it or just saw it and posted about it (we hypothesize it’s the latter).
We know the data were exposed no later than August 2026 and were secured shortly after September 28, 2026. We also know the messages in the files have date stamps consistent with the fact that slplsskdj2836v2jjsx[.]com was registered on September 1, 2026—the first date we see messages on that domain—and the aim6umein3kee[.]com domain was registered on August 25, 2025 — two days before the first message we see on that server. Both domains were registered with NameCheap and are behind Cloudflare.
We conclude that at least two entities must have downloaded the data — the researcher who contacted us and whoever else obtained the data that was leaked. We don’t know how many other researchers or others may have discovered the exposure and downloaded the files. We also don’t know when the exposure first began.
Did whoever secured the MongoDB instance on or about September 29  ever tell SRG’s top leadership that the instance was open for more than a month, or did someone try to cover up their mistake by not saying anything? SRG’s spokesperson claimed they had done a security audit. Did they leave their backup storage out of that audit, or did they not have adequate logs?

On October 5, 2026, Danish authorities announced a major data breach of the Denmark Central Person Register (CPR), the national population database. The incident exposed the personal data of approximately 8.8 million individuals, including current and former residents. The attackers did not exploit a technical vulnerability but instead abused the legitimate access credentials of a trusted third-party company. For about 10 days, the threat actors executed a high volume of automated queries to exfiltrate names, addresses, and the unique 10-digit CPR identification numbers. This breach is considered "deeply serious" by the Danish government due to the central role the CPR number plays in daily life, and a police investigation has been launched.

Threat Overview
The data breach occurred in September 2026 when an unidentified threat actor gained control over and misused the account of a private Danish company. This company had legitimate, authorized access to query the CPR system. Instead of hacking the CPR directly, the attackers leveraged this trusted relationship to harvest data at scale. This method is often referred to as a supply chain or third-party attack, where the target's security is circumvented by compromising a less secure partner.
The attackers performed a large number of automated queries over approximately 10 days, a pattern of activity that was flagged as unusual by the register's administration on October 2, 2026. The compromised data includes:

Full Names
Addresses
10-digit CPR numbers

The government has assured that individuals with protected name-and-address status were not affected by this breach.
Technical Analysis
The attack vector was the abuse of legitimate credentials, a form of T1078 - Valid Accounts. The attackers specifically exploited a T1199 - Trusted Relationship between the Danish government and the private company. The core of the data exfiltration was a 'smash and grab' operation using automated scripts to make a high volume of queries. This suggests the attackers focused on data collection rather than persistence or lateral movement within the CPR system itself.
The detection of the breach was based on anomaly detection, specifically the unusual surge in query volume from the compromised company's account. This highlights the importance of monitoring the behavior of even trusted, authorized users.
Impact Assessment
This is a highly significant data breach with severe potential consequences for the 8.8 million affected individuals. The CPR number is a national identification number in Denmark, used for nearly all interactions with public authorities and many private services like banking, healthcare, and insurance. The exposure of this number alongside names and addresses creates a critical risk of:

Identity Theft and Fraud: Criminals can use the data to impersonate individuals, open fraudulent accounts, or apply for loans.

Denmark's national CPR (Central Person Register) system, which contains personal information for all residents including names, addresses, CPR numbers, and other sensitive data, has been breached by unauthorized access.The breach, discovered on October 2, 2026, involved a private Danish company that had legal access to the system.

Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund urged residents to remain vigilant and avoid sharing passwords or confidential information with unsolicited callers or message senders.

text:
Data Breaches

Illustrative image generated with AI

A malware infection on a single employee computer at Nippon Columbia (NCG) has put the personal records of Daiichi Kosho's karaoke customers and employees at risk, according to BleepingComputer's report on Daiichi Kosho's disclosure. NCG is a contractor that handles customer data for the karaoke operator. Daiichi Kosho says it has not confirmed any theft or leak.
What Daiichi Kosho says was exposed
Daiichi Kosho puts the affected scope at 8,724,000 records in total. That breaks down into 8,631,000 customer records and 93,000 employee records. Each record may contain a full name, gender, date of birth, email address and telephone number.
Passwords are not part of the affected data, according to the company. It also says it has found no sign that loyalty points were used without authorization.
Daiichi Kosho describes itself as Japan's largest karaoke maker, with 521 venues nationwide, including the Big Echo chain. The customer data relates to these brands: BIG ECHO, MEGA BIG, Karaoke CLUB DAM, Banana Club, B-GARAGE and DK Dining.
Timeline and response
NCG told Daiichi Kosho on October 5 that it had found malware. It isolated the affected system the following day. Daiichi Kosho reports that NCG then reset passwords and other authentication credentials. NCG is also investigating the cause and scope of the incident, including whether any data has surfaced online.
Daiichi Kosho states that its own systems were not breached. The exposure sits entirely within the contractor's environment.
A later update, as described by BleepingComputer, added nothing further on whether data leaked. BleepingComputer found no public announcement from NCG and says it has contacted the company and is awaiting a reply.
What is still unknown
The reporting does not name the malware family, the way it reached the employee's computer, or any attacker or group. Whether data was actually stolen, leaked or sold is unconfirmed. What is established is the infection on one workstation and the scope of data that system could reach, as defined by Daiichi Kosho.
The two headline figures describe different scopes. About 8.6 million refers to customers alone (8,631,000), while the 8,724,000 total also includes the 93,000 employee records.
Guidance for customers
Daiichi Kosho advises customers to stay cautious given the potential risk. In practice, it recommends treating unsolicited email, SMS or phone contact with suspicion, particularly anything asking for payments or for sensitive personal or financial information. The exposed fields are enough to make such messages look personalized, so a message that uses a correct name or birth date is not proof of legitimacy.

Vitalik Buterin, the co-founder of Ethereum, has backed a warning from fellow researcher Justin Drake about the future of crypto security. Drake says artificial intelligence could break the cryptography behind Bitcoin and Ethereum before quantum computers ever do.
Drake posted his warning on Wednesday. He called for the industry to consider entering “bunker mode” by slowly moving funds to new wallet addresses.

Buterin responded directly to the post. He said people should not rush to move their funds right away.

“But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously,” Buterin wrote.

Why AI Has Researchers Worried
Drake’s concern follows a release from OpenAI this week. The company published 722 mathematical manuscripts produced by one of its internal models.
Last month, a group of 10,000 AI agents working together solved the Navier-Stokes equation. That is one of the hardest unsolved problems in math and physics, and the agents did it in 88 hours.

Drake said these results show how fast AI is moving in mathematics. He said elliptic curve cryptography, which protects Bitcoin and Ethereum wallets, could be an early target.

“Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks,” Drake wrote. He said hash functions are built to avoid that kind of structure, which may make them safer.

Buterin went further and said lattice-based cryptography, often seen as quantum-resistant, might not be safe either. He said this is one reason Ethereum’s long-term roadmap is moving toward hash-based systems.
Dragonfly managing partner Haseeb Qureshi also weighed in. He called Drake’s warning “a very sober call” and said the real risk is normal math, not quantum computing.
What Drake Is Asking Holders to Do
Drake’s main recommendation is moving crypto funds to fresh addresses whose public keys have never been exposed. A public key becomes visible once an address signs a transaction.
He said large and sophisticated holders should move first. Any funds left behind after a transaction should also be shifted to a new address.
Drake named several companies, including Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether. He asked them to consider stronger protection for cold storage funds.
He also pointed to Project Eleven’s Bitcoin Risq List. The list already tracks more than 14 million bitcoin addresses with exposed public keys.
Drake said wallets under 50 BTC get some cover from what he called “Satoshi’s shield.” About 20,000 addresses tied to Bitcoin’s creator each hold 50 BTC and would likely be targeted first.
Buterin supported the idea of using unused addresses, calling it “a good idea” if it is not difficult to do. He also shared a personal warning about the process itself.

“I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined,” Buterin wrote.

Drake agreed that any shift needs to be slow and careful. He said a rushed migration would cause more harm than the risk it is meant to prevent.
Drake said the long-term fix is what he calls “post-AI cryptography.” He said he favors systems built on hash functions rather than elliptic curves, and noted that Ethereum’s draft roadmap already points in that direction.

In environments studied for the 2026 State of Agent Security Report, roughly 1,280 third-party products now embed AI. About 282 of them sit behind single sign-on. The other thousand are invisible to identity infrastructure by default, not because anyone hid them, but because an identity stack can only govern what authenticates through it, and most agents never do.

That gap is the clearest expression of a shift the security industry is only starting to name. For several years, "AI security" solved a first-party problem: the company decided to use AI, procured licenses, deployed a model behind a gateway, and security pointed controls at the thing the business had chosen. Agents do not arrive that way. They arrive inside software the enterprise already runs, and they arrive without a decision.

Why the decision point mattered more than the controls

Every control in the first-party toolkit assumes a moment exists: model scanning assumes a model was selected, prompt inspection assumes a gateway was deployed, an acceptable-use policy assumes there was an adoption to accept. That moment gave security a review, a surface to instrument, and an owner to name.

Agents skip the moment. Salesforce's Slack Code, launched in August 2026, lets a user tag a coding agent into any conversation; the agent reads the shared context, writes the code, and opens the pull request. The announcement promises agents "inherit Slack's built-in security model, permissions, and admin controls from day one, without any additional IT lift." Read by a security team, that sentence describes an autonomous actor with reach into GitHub and production infrastructure whose governance is a chat tool's channel membership. There was nothing to instrument, because nothing was adopted.

Three launch vectors, one destination

Security leaders tend to sort agents into two buckets: bought and built. There is a third, and it is the largest. Inherited agents ship inside existing platforms via product updates. Configured agents are an enterprise's own prompts and logic running on someone else's runtime, model, and connectors. Built agents are open frameworks on infrastructure the enterprise owns end to end. The first two account for the overwhelming majority of adoption and are growing exponentially as every major application becomes an agent platform. The third is the smallest and slowest growing, and it is the only one with a repo to scan and a build to gate.

The destination is the same regardless of origin. An agent born in a CRM ends up reading a data warehouse and writing to a ticketing system. An agent assembled on a cloud platform ends up holding tokens into Salesforce, Slack, and Drive. The enterprise application layer is where they all execute, and it has no fixed edges.

Four questions that work on any agent

Every agent has two parts: the model that reasons and the scaffolding around it that turns a model into an actor, deciding what it is wired to, what it may call, and when it acts. Almost none of the risk lives in the model. It lives in the scaffolding and the ecosystem the scaffolding sits inside. Four questions cover it, and none of them ask what the model would do on its own.

What it looks like in practice

Identity

Is the agent registered anywhere? Does a named human raise a hand when asked "whose is this?" Or does it silently run as whoever built it?

SILENT RANSOM GROUP ALLEGEDLY EXTORTED $207 MILLION WITHOUT ENCRYPTING FILES
Pierluigi Paganini

October 10, 2026
Silent Ransom Group allegedly extorted $207 million from 27 law firms in six months using phone calls and social engineering, not encryption.

Silent Ransom Group doesn’t rely on encryption. No malware payload, no locked files, just phone calls and social engineering aimed almost entirely at law firms, and apparently it works extraordinarily well. A new leak of the group’s internal chats, first shared with DataBreaches by researcher Tammy Harper, backs that up with numbers.

The leaked data comes from two of the group’s servers and covers about 13 months, from August 2025 to September 2026. It contains 5,692 chat messages about ransom negotiations, ways to access victims’ systems, and plans for future targets.

“The leak was first shared with this site by Tammy Harper as an onion site with 5,692 chat messages that discuss victim payments, possible access methods, approaches to future victims, the purchase of an apartment in Moscow by one of the members, and discussions of guns and drones, among other topics.” reads the report published by DataBreaches.

The chats also discuss personal matters, including one member buying an apartment in Moscow, as well as guns and drones. The conversations sound less like a secret criminal operation and more like a sales team sharing tips on how to make money.

The group’s internal records claim that 27 law firms paid around $207 million in ransom payments between April and September 2026. Crystal Intelligence examined the cryptocurrency transactions and money laundering activity, concluding that blockchain data supports the overall scale of the operation but does not confirm the exact amounts.
